Do we use AI, or does AI use us?
Press enter or click to view image in full size

It’s a question worth sitting with before answering too quickly. Every generation has adopted tools that changed how it thinks — the calculator, the search engine, the spell-checker. But there’s a difference between a tool that assists thinking and a tool that replaces the act of thinking itself. When the discomfort of not knowing something has an instant escape button on your smartphone, we stop building the one skill the labor market will never be able to automate: learning how to think.
I live this, and I feel it, up close. More than twenty years teaching, close to five thousand students who have passed through my classes, and I can say with certainty that the essay a college student hands me today doesn’t read the way it did five years ago. It’s more polished, more symmetrical, almost always correct. And yet, when I ask them in class to defend what they wrote out loud — to explain why they chose that argument and not another — the silence that follows says everything. It’s not that they don’t know the topic. It’s that they didn’t think it through themselves: they generated it. And there’s an enormous difference between those two things, even when the final product looks identical on paper.
The Brown University Experiment
